topics.description: A gut feeling that some sample outputs 'look fine' is not testing. A real **evaluation set** catches problems before your users do.

lesson.summary: A gut feeling that some sample outputs 'look fine' is not testing. A real **evaluation set** catches problems before your users do.
lesson.content:
## Evaluating LLM Apps: Why 'It Looks Good to Me' Isn't Good Enough

> **Core Concept:** A gut feeling that some sample outputs 'look fine' is not testing. A real **evaluation set** catches problems before your users do.

### Why It Matters
- LLM output is ==not deterministic==, so a small prompt tweak can quietly break something that used to work fine.
- Testing a handful of prompts by eye tells you almost nothing about the thousands of weird, edge-case-y prompts real users will actually send.
- Without a fixed set of cases and criteria, you cannot tell whether a change made your app better or worse. You can only guess.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine a driving instructor who decides a student is ready for their license
after watching them make one smooth left turn in an empty parking lot. That
single turn told the instructor almost nothing about how the student handles
merging onto a highway, parallel parking, or a sudden stop in traffic. A real
driving test covers a fixed set of specific situations on purpose, precisely
because "it looked fine once" is not the same as "it reliably works."


### Key Engineering Principles
- It is easy to type a handful of test prompts, glance at the answers, think 'yeah, that looks right,' and ship it. That habit is the single most common reason LLM features regress quietly in production.
- A model's behavior on five prompts you happened to try tells you almost nothing about its behavior on the full range of real user input, because the space of things people actually type is enormous and unpredictable.
- A real **evaluation set** is a representative batch of realistic inputs, plus deliberate edge cases like empty input, very long input, adversarial input, or ambiguous requests that could reasonably be answered two different ways.
- Each case in the set needs a defined idea of a good answer, whether that's an exact expected output, a checklist a human reviews, or a rule an automated grader checks, so a score means the same thing every time it is run.
- Graders fall into three broad kinds: exact or rule-based checks (does the output contain a required phrase, pass a regex, parse as valid JSON), human review against a rubric, and **'LLM as judge'**, where a separate model call scores the output against written criteria at a scale humans cannot match.
- LLM-as-judge is powerful but ==not free of bias==. It can be fooled by confident-sounding wrong answers or by outputs that are simply longer, so its scores are worth spot-checking against human judgment, especially early on.
- Every time you change your prompt, swap a model, or adjust retrieval, you rerun the whole set and see whether your score moved, instead of guessing from vibes. ==Changing more than one thing at once== makes a score drop impossible to attribute.
- This matters more for LLM apps than typical software because output is not deterministic, the same prompt can produce a different answer on two separate calls, so silent regressions are common without a real evaluation habit.
- Aggregate scores can hide the real story. A 2 percent score drop that is actually a total failure on one important category of input looks the same as a 2 percent drop spread evenly, unless you break the score down by category.
- An evaluation set turns 'I think this change made it better' into 'I can show you it made it better,' which is the difference between shipping on a hunch and shipping on evidence.

topics.title: Feature Engineering: The Inputs You Choose Matter as Much as the Model
topics.description: A model can only be as good as the inputs you feed it. **Shaping those inputs well** is often worth more than switching to a fancier model.

lesson.summary: A model can only be as good as the inputs you feed it. **Shaping those inputs well** is often worth more than switching to a fancier model.
lesson.content:
## Feature Engineering: The Inputs You Choose Matter as Much as the Model

> **Core Concept:** A model can only be as good as the inputs you feed it. **Shaping those inputs well** is often worth more than switching to a fancier model.

### Why It Matters
- Raw data almost never arrives already shaped to reveal the pattern a model needs to learn.
- Some columns hide useful signal in a form the model cannot easily use, like a raw timestamp.
- Reaching for a bigger, fancier model is often a ==weaker fix== than simply improving the inputs.

### Intuitive Analogy
Picture two chefs cooking the exact same recipe. One walks into the market and
grabs whatever's closest, bruised tomatoes, wilted basil, a random cheese. The
other carefully picks ripe tomatoes, fragrant fresh basil, and a cheese that
actually complements the dish. Hand both chefs identical skill and the same
stove, and the second one's meal wins every time, not because they cooked
differently, but because they chose better ingredients before cooking even
started. Feature engineering is picking your ingredients with that same care,
before the model ever gets involved.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A **feature** is any piece of information you feed into a model, like age, price, or days since last login. The set of all features for one example is often called a feature vector.
- **Feature engineering** is reshaping, combining, and creating inputs that make the real pattern easier for the model to find, it happens before training, not during it.
- Transforming a single column can help, like turning a raw timestamp into 'hour of the day,' or a free-text city name into a 'distance from headquarters' number the model can actually use.
- Combining columns can help too, like turning 'total spent' and 'number of visits' into 'average spend per visit,' a ratio that carries more direct signal than either raw column alone.
- Categorical columns, like 'color' or 'country,' usually need to become numbers before most models can use them. **One-hot encoding** turns each category into its own 0/1 column, avoiding the false sense of order a plain number would imply.
- Numeric features often need scaling, like **standardization** (subtracting the mean, dividing by the standard deviation) or **min-max scaling** (squeezing values into a 0 to 1 range), so that no single feature dominates just because its raw numbers happen to be larger.
- Removing pure-noise features, or ones that leak the answer in a way that won't exist at prediction time, matters just as much as adding good ones, extra irrelevant columns give a model more chances to latch onto spurious patterns.
- **Binning** turns a continuous number into buckets, like turning exact age into '18-25,' '26-35,' and so on, which can help a model that struggles to find a smooth relationship but loses some precision in the process.
- A simple model fed thoughtfully engineered features often beats a complex model fed raw, unprocessed data, because the complex model still has to ==rediscover the same pattern from scratch==, using more data and risking more overfitting along the way.
- Experienced practitioners spend more time asking 'what would actually help here' than tuning model settings, feature engineering is usually where the real performance gains hide, not in swapping algorithms.

topics.description: Show the model a couple of **worked examples**, and ask it to think in steps, and its answers get noticeably more reliable.

lesson.summary: Show the model a couple of **worked examples**, and ask it to think in steps, and its answers get noticeably more reliable.
lesson.content:
## Few-Shot Examples and Chain of Thought: Teaching by Showing, Not Just Telling

> **Core Concept:** Show the model a couple of **worked examples**, and ask it to think in steps, and its answers get noticeably more reliable.

### Why It Matters
- A plain instruction with no examples leaves the model guessing at the exact format, tone, or nuance you actually want.
- Language models generate one word at a time, so a rushed answer to a multi-step problem is more likely to ==skip a step== or slip on the arithmetic.
- A written description of a pattern is often less reliable than just showing the pattern in action.

### Intuitive Analogy
Picture training a new cashier. You could hand them a rulebook and walk away,
or you could ring up three sample transactions together first, one with a
coupon, one with a return, one with a split payment, and talk through each
step out loud as you go. The second cashier makes far fewer mistakes on their
first solo shift, not because they are smarter, but because they have seen
the pattern in action and watched the reasoning, not just the final total.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A '**zero-shot**' prompt asks the model to do a task with no examples, just an instruction. Fine for simple, common tasks the model has seen the shape of thousands of times during training.
- A '**few-shot**' prompt includes two or three example input-output pairs before the real question, and the model mirrors the pattern it sees, a form of **in-context learning** where nothing about the model itself changes, only what is in the prompt this one time.
- Few-shot examples are often more reliable than a written description of the pattern, because the model imitates the shape directly instead of translating your description of a format into that format itself, which is an extra place for errors to creep in.
- The order and consistency of few-shot examples matters. ==Examples that vary in format from each other==, or that are arranged inconsistently, teach the model a blurrier pattern than a small, clean, uniform set.
- **Chain of thought** asks the model to reason step by step before giving a final answer, instead of jumping straight to it, usually triggered by phrasing like 'think step by step' or by including worked reasoning inside your few-shot examples.
- Because a language model generates one token at a time with no scratch space, chain of thought effectively gives it a scratch space: each reasoning token it writes becomes part of the context the next token is conditioned on, which is why reasoning out loud measurably improves accuracy on multi-step problems.
- Combining both means writing your few-shot examples so the reasoning is visible inside them too, not just the final answer, this is often called **few-shot chain of thought**, and it teaches the model both the answer format and the reasoning style at once.
- **Zero-shot chain of thought**, just adding 'think step by step' with no examples at all, often recovers a large chunk of the benefit of full few-shot chain of thought at a fraction of the prompt length.
- More examples is not automatically better. ==Past roughly three to five well-chosen examples==, additional ones usually cost tokens and latency without meaningfully improving reliability.
- Neither trick is magic. ==A model that fundamentally does not know a fact will not learn it from your examples==, both techniques shape format and reasoning style, they do not inject new knowledge the model was never trained on.

topics.title: Fine-Tuning and LoRA: Specializing a Model Without Rebuilding It
topics.description: **Fine-tuning** takes a general model and specializes it for your exact use case, and **LoRA** is a lightweight way to do that without retraining the whole thing.

lesson.summary: **Fine-tuning** takes a general model and specializes it for your exact use case, and **LoRA** is a lightweight way to do that without retraining the whole thing.
lesson.content:
## Fine-Tuning and LoRA: Specializing a Model Without Rebuilding It

> **Core Concept:** **Fine-tuning** takes a general model and specializes it for your exact use case, and **LoRA** is a lightweight way to do that without retraining the whole thing.

### Why It Matters
- A general purpose model is decent at almost everything and perfectly tuned for nothing in particular.
- ==Full fine-tuning== updates every parameter in a model that can have billions of them, which costs huge amounts of compute, memory, and storage.
- Teams often want several specialized versions of the same base model, and storing a full copy of the weights for each one gets expensive fast.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of a general model like a doctor fresh out of medical school. They know
a broad amount about the whole human body, but they're not yet a cardiologist
or a dermatologist. Fine-tuning is like a residency: focused, extra training
on one narrow specialty, using the general medical knowledge as a foundation
rather than starting from zero. Full fine-tuning is like sending that doctor
through years of intense specialty training that reshapes almost everything
they know. LoRA is more like handing them a very good specialty textbook and a
few months of focused practice: they come out noticeably better at the
specialty, without having relearned all of medicine from scratch.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A general purpose language model is trained on a huge, broad slice of text, which makes it decent broadly but not specialized in anything, and fine-tuning is the process of continuing to train that model on new data to shift it toward one narrower job.
- Fine-tuning trains that general model further on a smaller, focused dataset specific to your task, like support transcripts or legal documents in one niche, using the same training process, just with different data and usually a much smaller learning rate.
- Fine-tuning picks up the vocabulary, tone, response format, and patterns specific to that narrower world. It shapes how the model behaves, not what facts it has access to.
- Full fine-tuning updates every one of the model's internal parameters, which is expensive in compute, memory, and storage, and for a model with billions of parameters, storing one complete fine-tuned copy per use case adds up fast.
- **LoRA**, short for Low-Rank Adaptation, is based on the observation that the change needed to specialize a model can usually be captured by a much smaller set of numbers than the full parameter count, without losing much quality.
- LoRA **freezes** the original parameters completely and inserts small pairs of new matrices alongside select layers of the model, typically the attention layers, and only those new matrices get trained.
- The 'low-rank' part refers to the shape of those inserted matrices: instead of learning a full-size update to a huge weight matrix, LoRA learns two much smaller matrices whose product approximates that update, which is why the trainable parameter count can drop by **over 99 percent**.
- Because a LoRA add-on is small, often just megabytes instead of gigabytes, you can keep several of them and swap between specialties on the same frozen base model, loading a different add-on per request instead of hosting a separate full model per specialty.
- A LoRA add-on can even be merged back into the base model's weights after training if you want a single deployable artifact, or kept separate if you want to keep swapping it.
- **Step 1, data collection**: gather 50 to a few thousand examples of the exact input-output behavior you want, formatted as role-tagged conversations (system, user, assistant). For a narrow behavior, quality and consistency beat volume, 100 clean, consistent examples usually beat 1,000 messy or contradictory ones. Three realistic sources: write them by hand for full control at small scale, use a stronger model to draft candidates that a human then edits and approves for medium scale, or mine and clean real transcripts you already have (support tickets, chat logs) while stripping anything private.
- **Step 2, formatting**: save the dataset as JSONL, one JSON object per line, each with a list of role-tagged messages matching the base model's chat template exactly. Hold out roughly 10 to 20 percent of examples as a validation split before training even starts, never after, so that split stays untouched by anything the model sees during training.
- **Step 3, environment setup**: for a consumer GPU, load the frozen base model in 4-bit using **QLoRA** (via the bitsandbytes library), which quantizes the huge frozen weights to save memory while the small LoRA matrices still train in full precision. This is what makes fine-tuning a 7B-parameter model realistic on a single consumer GPU with 8 to 12GB of memory instead of needing a data-center card.
- **Step 4, configure LoRA**: pick a **rank** (commonly 8 to 64, start at 8 or 16 for a narrow behavior), set **lora_alpha** to roughly twice the rank as a starting default, and choose **target_modules**, typically the attention projection layers (q_proj, v_proj, and often k_proj and o_proj too). Targeting more modules or a higher rank gives the adapter more capacity to learn, at the cost of more trainable parameters and higher overfitting risk on a small dataset.
- **Step 5, train**: run the training loop (commonly with the trl library's SFTTrainer, which handles the chat-formatted supervised fine-tuning loop directly) for a small number of epochs, often 1 to 5 for a narrow behavior. Use a small per-device batch size (1 to 4) combined with gradient accumulation to simulate a larger effective batch size without running out of memory, and watch training loss versus validation loss every so often, not just at the very end.
- **Step 6, evaluate and ship**: after training, chat with the result using prompts phrased differently from anything in the training set, this is the real test of whether it learned a pattern rather than memorized examples. Then either keep the adapter as a small separate file to load on demand, or call a merge function to fold it into the base weights for one single deployable model.

lesson.content:
## From One Perceptron to a Whole Network

> **Core Concept:** One perceptron can only draw a straight line. Stack many of them in **layers**, and together they can carve out shapes as tangled as you need.

### Why It Matters
- A single perceptron can only separate data with ==one straight cut==, so real-world patterns with curved or tangled boundaries defeat it immediately.
- You need a way to combine many simple opinions into one richer judgment, without hand-designing how they interact.
- As problems get more complex, you need a structure that scales up smoothly instead of needing a totally new idea every time.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think about how a single food critic reviews a restaurant. One person, one
opinion, one straightforward verdict based on whatever they personally
weigh most (maybe they're obsessed with plating and don't care about
price). Now imagine an entire panel of critics, each with their own quirky
preferences, whose individual verdicts get fed to a head critic who weighs
all of their opinions together into a final score. That panel can catch
nuances no single critic ever could, because each member notices something
different, and the head critic combines those different angles into a
richer judgment.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A single perceptron can only separate data along one straight cut, so anything more complicated than 'everything on this side is yes' trips it up, no matter how it's trained.
- The fix isn't a smarter perceptron, it's more of them, arranged in layers, each layer built from many units working side by side.
- A **layer** is a group of perceptron-like units that all look at the same inputs at once, each with its own independent set of weights, each forming its own weighted opinion in parallel.
- Stacking layers means one layer's outputs become the next layer's inputs, the way a head critic weighs the panel's scores rather than tasting the food directly. Nothing about the math changes, only what counts as 'the input' at each stage.
- Layers between the raw input and the final output are called **hidden layers**, because you never observe their outputs directly, you only see the final layer's output.
- This design is called a **feedforward network**, or multilayer perceptron, because information flows in one direction only, from input toward output, with no loops feeding a later layer's output back into an earlier one.
- Each hidden unit specializes in noticing a different pattern in the data, purely as a side effect of starting from different random weights and receiving different gradient updates during training, nobody assigns units their specialty by hand.
- The **width** of a layer is how many units it contains, and the **depth** of a network is how many layers it has. Both dimensions add capacity, but in different ways: width lets a layer detect more distinct patterns at once, depth lets patterns build on top of each other.
- A network with enough units and layers can approximate almost any pattern, curved boundaries included, not just straight lines. This is formalized as the **universal approximation theorem**, though in practice getting a network to actually find good weights for a hard pattern is ==a separate challenge entirely==.
- Every connection between layers, meaning every line from one unit to another, has its own independent weight, which is why network size is usually described by counting parameters, not just neurons.

topics.title: Function Calling: Giving a Model a Menu of Tools It Can Actually Use
topics.description: **Function calling** lets you hand a model a menu of tools it's allowed to use, and the model decides on its own when calling one of them is the right move.

lesson.summary: **Function calling** lets you hand a model a menu of tools it's allowed to use, and the model decides on its own when calling one of them is the right move.
lesson.content:
## Function Calling: Giving a Model a Menu of Tools It Can Actually Use

> **Core Concept:** **Function calling** lets you hand a model a menu of tools it's allowed to use, and the model decides on its own when calling one of them is the right move.

### Why It Matters
- On its own, a language model can only produce **text**. It cannot check today's weather, look up a real order, or reliably do exact arithmetic on huge numbers.
- A model has no live connection to the outside world, only patterns learned from the text it was trained on.
- Without a defined way to call real code, an LLM assistant can only talk about doing things, never ==actually do them==.

### Intuitive Analogy
Picture a hotel concierge. A guest doesn't need to know how to book a
restaurant table, call a cab, or print a boarding pass themselves. They just
tell the concierge what they need, and the concierge, who has a fixed list of
services available at the front desk, picks the right one and handles it.
The concierge doesn't invent a new service on the spot, they choose from the
menu pinned behind the desk and use exactly the one that fits the request.


### Key Engineering Principles
- You describe a set of tools to the model ahead of time, each with a name, a description of what it does, and a schema of the inputs it expects, like get_weather(city: string), usually written in a structured format such as JSON schema.
- The model does not run these tools itself. It decides whether one is relevant to the user's request and, if so, outputs a **structured request**, not free text, naming the tool and the arguments to call it with.
- Your **application code** is the part that actually executes the function, using the inputs the model chose, which means your code, not the model, controls what is genuinely allowed to happen.
- The result of running the tool gets serialized back into the conversation as a new message, and the model reads that result and uses it to write the final answer, sometimes deciding it needs to call another tool first.
- The full loop: user asks a question, model decides a tool is needed and which one, your code runs that tool and gets a real result, the model reads the result and either answers or calls another tool. This can chain across multiple tool calls before a final answer appears.
- Tool selection is driven entirely by the name, description, and parameter schema you write, the model has no other information about what a tool actually does under the hood.
- This is what allows an LLM assistant to feel like it can 'do things' instead of just talk about things, effectively giving a text-only model hands, as long as those hands are tools you explicitly built and exposed.
- A model can only use tools it was explicitly given access to in that request. It cannot invent new ones on the spot, no matter how plausible a made-up function name might look in its output, so ==never trust an unlisted tool call==.
- Structured output and function calling share the same underlying idea: instead of the model producing loose prose, you constrain it to produce a specific, parseable shape your code can act on directly.

topics.title: GANs: A Forger and a Detective, Locked in a Room Together
topics.description: A **GAN** is two networks fighting each other, one making fakes and one spotting them, and the fight is exactly what makes the fakes get good.

lesson.summary: A **GAN** is two networks fighting each other, one making fakes and one spotting them, and the fight is exactly what makes the fakes get good.
lesson.content:
## GANs: A Forger and a Detective, Locked in a Room Together

> **Core Concept:** A **GAN** is two networks fighting each other, one making fakes and one spotting them, and the fight is exactly what makes the fakes get good.

### Why It Matters
- Nobody can hand a model a precise rulebook for what makes an image 'realistic,' the concept is too fuzzy to code by hand.
- A model trained only to copy exact examples tends to produce blurry, safe, unconvincing averages instead of sharp, specific results.
- Generating convincing new examples needs some kind of feedback signal even when there is no fixed correct answer to check against.

### Intuitive Analogy
Picture an art forger and an art detective stuck in the same small room for
months. The forger paints a copy of a famous painting and hands it over. The
detective studies it and says "fake, the brushstrokes are too clean." The
forger goes back, tries again, learns from that specific mistake, and comes
back with something better. The detective studies harder too, picking up on
subtler tells each round. Neither one ever "wins" completely, but after enough
rounds locked in that room, the forger's paintings become so convincing that
even the detective, now an expert, can only guess.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A GAN is built from two separate neural networks trained at the same time, working against each other on purpose, an idea called adversarial training.
- The **generator** is the forger. It takes a vector of random noise as input and transforms it, through its layers, into a fake, for example an image, learning over time which transformations tend to fool the discriminator.
- The **discriminator** is the detective. It is really just a binary classifier: it looks at one image at a time, real or fake mixed together in training batches, and outputs a single probability that the image is real.
- Training alternates in rounds, not all at once: first the discriminator's weights update to get better at telling real from fake on the current batch, then the generator's weights update based on how well its latest fakes fooled that discriminator.
- The generator never sees real images directly. Everything it learns about what 'realistic' looks like is filtered entirely through the discriminator's judgments, which is the whole trick that avoids needing a human-written rulebook.
- Each side only ever reacts to how good the other side currently is, so both are forced to keep sharpening in a moving target dynamic, similar to an arms race where standing still means falling behind.
- The ideal end state, called equilibrium, is when the generator's fakes are statistically indistinguishable from real data and the discriminator can do no better than a coin flip at telling them apart.
- Training can go badly in specific, well documented ways. ==Mode collapse== happens when the generator finds one trick, or a narrow handful of outputs, that reliably fools the current discriminator, and keeps repeating it instead of covering the full diversity of real data.
- ==Vanishing gradients== are another failure mode: if the discriminator gets too good too fast, it rejects every fake with near total confidence, which gives the generator almost no useful signal about how to improve.
- Conditional GANs extend the basic idea by feeding the generator and discriminator an extra label or class alongside the noise, letting you request a specific category of output, like 'generate a fake shirt' instead of 'generate a fake something.'

topics.title: From Judging to Creating: What Generative AI Actually Does
topics.description: Every model you've met so far looks at something and decides what it is. **Generative models** look at nothing and decide what to make.

lesson.summary: Every model you've met so far looks at something and decides what it is. **Generative models** look at nothing and decide what to make.
lesson.content:
## From Judging to Creating: What Generative AI Actually Does

> **Core Concept:** Every model you've met so far looks at something and decides what it is. **Generative models** look at nothing and decide what to make.

### Why It Matters
- Judging existing content (spam or not, cat or dog) does not help you produce brand new content that never existed before.
- Businesses and creators increasingly want new images, text, audio, and designs on demand, not just labels for content they already have.
- A model that only draws boundaries between categories has no built-in notion of how to generate a fresh, plausible example.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think about the difference between a movie critic and a screenwriter. The critic
watches a finished film and tells you whether it is good, bad, a comedy, or a
thriller. That is judgment. The screenwriter starts from a blank page and
produces something that never existed before. Both people understand movies
deeply, but only one of them creates. Everything you have studied up to this
lesson, classifiers that spot spam or sort images, has been training critics.
Now we start training screenwriters.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A classifier's job is to take something that already exists, a photo, an email, a sentence, and output a label. It is a narrowing operation, collapsing a rich input down to one of a small set of answers.
- A generative model runs the tape the other way. It starts with almost nothing, often random noise or a short prompt, and expands that starting point into something rich and specific, an image, a sentence, a sound.
- This shift changes what 'learning' means at a mathematical level. A discriminative model learns a decision boundary, essentially a dividing line that separates categories in the space of possible inputs.
- A generative model instead learns a **probability distribution**, roughly how likely any given example is to be a real member of the category it was trained on, across every possible variation, not just the ones it saw directly.
- Once a model has learned that distribution well, generating something new is just sampling from it, picking a point according to how likely the model thinks it is, which tends to produce something that feels as plausible as real examples without literally copying any one of them.
- There is no single way to build a generative model. Three approaches matter most today, each solving the sampling problem differently: VAEs, GANs, and diffusion models.
- VAEs learn to compress something down to a compact latent representation and rebuild new variations by decoding random points from a deliberately smoothed version of that compressed space.
- GANs pit two networks against each other, a generator and a discriminator, until the generator gets frighteningly good at producing fakes the discriminator can no longer reliably catch.
- Diffusion models learn a much narrower skill, removing a small amount of noise from a noisy image, and generate by applying that skill repeatedly starting from pure static.
- These three approaches trade off differently: VAEs train the most stably but tend to produce ==slightly blurrier results==, GANs can produce sharp results but are ==trickier to train==, and diffusion models are currently the most reliable at high quality but ==need many steps== to generate a single output.

topics.title: Git Basics: Version Control for AI Projects
topics.description: Git is not just for saving code. In AI work it is how you remember which version of your model actually worked.

lesson.summary: Git is not just for saving code. In AI work it is how you remember which version of your model actually worked.
lesson.content:
## Git Basics: Version Control for AI Projects

> **Core Concept:** Git is not just for saving code. In AI work it is how you remember which version of your model actually worked.

### Why It Matters
- Without any history, overwriting a file destroys the only record of what used to work.
- AI projects change constantly, code, data, and hyperparameters, so 'what did I change' becomes a real question fast.
- Trying something risky directly on the working version puts the thing that already works at risk.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think about a video game with a save file system. You save before a tough boss
fight, try something risky, and if it goes wrong you reload the last save
instead of starting the whole game over. Git is that save system for your
project. Every commit is a checkpoint you can return to, compare against, or
branch off from, whether the "boss fight" is a tricky bug or a training run
that mysteriously stopped improving.


### Key Engineering Principles
- In regular software, Git tracks code changes: fix a bug, add a feature, commit, repeat. Under the hood, each commit stores a snapshot of every tracked file at that moment, not just a list of edits, which is why checking out an old commit restores the whole project instantly.
- AI projects add a second thing worth tracking just as carefully: experiments, meaning which script, data, and settings produced which result. A model that performs well is only reproducible if you know exactly what code and configuration produced it.
- A commit is a labeled snapshot of your project at one point in time, not a save-forever decision. You can always go back, compare, or undo, which is exactly what removes the fear of trying something risky.
- You should commit whenever you reach a state worth returning to, like code that runs or a script right before you change the learning rate. Small, frequent commits give you far more places to safely land than one giant commit at the end of the day.
- A good commit message explains why the change happened, since the diff already shows what changed. 'Why' is the part that disappears from your memory in a week, the diff never does.
- Branches let you try something risky without touching the version that already works. A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit, creating one is instant and nearly free, so there is no reason to hesitate before making one.
- If an experiment on a branch does not pan out, you delete the branch and the working version was never at risk. This is the entire point of branching: risk is contained, not eliminated.
- Merging brings a branch's changes back into another branch. If the two branches changed the same lines differently, Git flags a conflict and asks you to decide which version, or combination, is correct, it does not guess for you.
- A remote is a copy of the repository hosted elsewhere, like GitHub. Pushing sends your commits there, pulling brings down commits others made, and this is how a commit history becomes a shared, backed-up record instead of a local-only one.
- Staging, the step where you choose exactly which changes go into the next commit, lets you build a focused commit instead of bundling every unrelated edit currently sitting in your working directory.

- Merging brings a branch's changes back into another branch. If the two branches changed the same lines differently, Git flags a conflict and asks you to decide which version, or combination, is correct, it does not guess for you.
- A remote is a copy of the repository hosted elsewhere, like GitHub. Pushing sends your commits there, pulling brings down commits others made, and this is how a commit history becomes a shared, backed-up record instead of a local-only one.
- Staging, the step where you choose exactly which changes go into the next commit, lets you build a focused commit instead of bundling every unrelated edit currently sitting in your working directory.

callout.title: Engineering Principle
callout.text: Git is not just for saving code. In AI work it is how you remember which version of your model actually worked.

lesson.content:
## Giving Agents Memory Beyond One Conversation

> **Core Concept:** Without memory, an agent forgets everything the moment the task ends. **Short-term memory** gets it through the current job, **long-term memory** lets it get better over time.

### Why It Matters
- A language model has ==no built-in memory between separate runs==, so every new conversation starts as a total blank slate.
- Without holding onto what happened a few steps ago, an agent cannot keep a single **multi-step task** coherent.
- Without memory that survives past one session, an agent relearns the same facts and preferences over and over and never improves at working with a specific person.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think about a substitute teacher versus the regular teacher at a school.
The substitute walks in, has to be told everything fresh, which kids sit
where, what the class already covered, what worked last time, because they
have no memory of this classroom at all. They can still teach today's lesson
fine, that's short-term memory in action, holding onto what happens in the
room for the length of one class period. The regular teacher, though,
remembers that one student struggles with word problems, that a certain
seating chart causes chaos, and that a lesson bombed last year and needs
reworking. That's long-term memory, carried across many different days, not
just one class.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A language model on its own doesn't remember anything between separate runs. Each new conversation is a blank slate, it has ==no persistent state of its own==, only whatever text it is fed in that request.
- **Short-term memory** is what an agent keeps track of during the current task: what it already tried, what a tool just returned, what the plan looks like so far. It is the working memory for a single job.
- Short-term memory usually lives in the conversation itself, meaning the growing history of messages, or in working notes the agent keeps handy, and it disappears once the task wraps up.
- **Long-term memory** is information kept around across many separate tasks or sessions: a user's preferences, facts learned last week, patterns in what tends to go wrong. It is meant to outlive any single conversation.
- Long-term memory is usually stored somewhere outside the conversation entirely, like a database or a file, and pulled back in when relevant rather than kept in every prompt at all times.
- **Retrieval** is the step of deciding which stored long-term memories are actually relevant right now and pulling only those into context, since dumping everything ever stored would overwhelm the model and slow it down.
- Without long-term memory, an agent relearns the same things repeatedly and never actually improves at working with you specifically, every session feels like meeting it for the first time.
- The two aren't competing. Short-term memory keeps one task coherent while it happens, long-term memory is what turns disconnected tasks into something that feels like it knows you.
- **Context window** limits are the practical reason short-term memory can't just grow forever within a task. Older, less relevant details eventually have to be summarized or dropped to leave room for new information.
- A common real design keeps a rolling short-term window for the active task, and periodically writes a **compressed summary** of what happened out to long-term storage before that window gets trimmed.
